prompt: A company is considering outsourcing core manufacturing to a new overseas supplier to cut costs. Identify the top risks using the data given and recommend a risk-mitigation structure (not a go/no-go decision).
context: Supplier quote: 28% lower unit cost than current in-house production. Supplier due diligence (conducted by a third-party auditor) found the supplier is financially stable but has been in operation only 3 years and has no prior experience manufacturing this specific product category. Shipping lead time from the supplier's location adds 5 weeks versus current in-house lead time. The product line in question has historically had volatile demand, with month-to-month volume swings of +/-35% in the last 2 years (internal sales data).

binaryCriteria.description: Identifies the supplier's lack of experience in this specific product category as a quality/ramp-up risk, distinct from its financial stability.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer conflates financial stability with product-category competence, or omits this risk.

binaryCriteria.description: Connects the 5-week longer lead time to the historical +/-35% monthly demand volatility to identify a stockout/excess-inventory risk.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if lead time and demand volatility are discussed as separate, unconnected facts rather than combined into a single supply-responsiveness risk.

binaryCriteria.description: Recommends a phased or dual-sourcing mitigation structure (e.g., partial volume shift, retained in-house buffer capacity) rather than a full immediate switch or a simple go/no-go answer.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer only gives a go/no-go recommendation without a mitigation structure, since the prompt explicitly asks for the latter.

goldNotes: A strong answer identifies quality/ramp-up risk (supplier has no experience in this specific product category, despite financial stability) and demand-responsiveness risk (a 5-week longer lead time combined with historically +/-35% monthly demand swings creates a real risk of stockouts or excess inventory, since the supplier cannot react as quickly as in-house production could) as the two dominant risks — cost savings (28%) should not be the focus since the prompt asks for risks, not the business case. It should recommend a mitigation structure such as a phased/dual-sourcing approach (e.g., start with a smaller share of volume or a less demand-volatile SKU subset while monitoring quality, keep some in-house capacity as a buffer for demand spikes) rather than either fully committing immediately or rejecting outright (the prompt explicitly asks for a mitigation structure, not a go/no-go call).
